column2: What is the main question in a significance test?
column3: Did the sample groups have the same size?
column4: Could chance alone create a result this strong?
column5: Did the treatment change every individual value?
column6: Could a larger sample remove all uncertainty?

column2: If a treatment has no real effect what difference should be expected over many random assignments?
column3: A difference centered near zero should appear.
column4: A difference matching the claim should appear.
column5: A difference with no spread should appear.
column6: A difference far from zero should appear.

column2: Why is an observed sample difference by itself not convincing evidence?
column3: The sample difference must equal the parameter.
column4: The sample difference must be positive every time.
column5: The sample difference must come from a census.
column6: Chance variation can also create sample differences.

column2: Which pair of explanations is compared in a significance test?
column3: One says the sample was biased and one says it was random.
column4: One says the graph is symmetric and one says it is skewed.
column5: One says chance explains it and one says the treatment does.
column6: One says the mean is large and one says it is small.

column2: Before concluding a claim is convincing what must be estimated?
column3: The chance of a result this extreme under no effect.
column4: The exact size of the effect in the population.
column5: The percentage of subjects who liked the treatment.
column6: The number of future samples needed for certainty.

column2: Why does a randomization simulation begin with a no effect assumption?
column3: It forces each simulated mean to equal the sample mean.
column4: It builds a model of what chance alone could produce.
column5: It guarantees the observed statistic will be repeated.
column6: It removes the need to compare the two groups.

column2: In a re-randomization simulation what is shuffled from trial to trial?
column3: The study question is shuffled across the subjects.
column4: The sample means are shuffled across the trials.
column5: The population values are shuffled across the graph.
column6: The group labels are shuffled across the responses.

column2: Why are the original response values kept in the simulation?
column3: They make every simulated group the same size.
column4: They prove the observed effect is not random.
column5: They keep the study outcomes fixed while labels change.
column6: They guarantee the randomization graph stays narrow.

column2: What does one dot in a randomization distribution represent?
column3: One observed response from the original study.
column4: One simulated statistic from one shuffled assignment.
column5: One exact parameter value from the population.
column6: One confidence level from the chosen procedure.

column2: What does the tail area of the randomization distribution estimate?
column3: The proportion of simulated results this extreme or more.
column4: The proportion of subjects assigned to each group.
column5: The proportion of graphs that look approximately normal.
column6: The proportion of future studies with no variation.

column2: What does a very small tail proportion from the simulation tell us?
column3: It must have come from a flawed study design.
column4: It shows the treatment effect is very large.
column5: It proves the no effect model can never be true.
column6: It would be unusual if chance alone were operating.

column2: If the estimated chance is very small what is the best conclusion?
column3: Keep the chance-only explanation as equally likely.
column4: State that every subject responded the same way.
column5: Treat the sample result as evidence against no effect.
column6: Assume the treatment works for every population.

column2: Which statement is a common misconception after a very small chance value?
column3: A very small chance value proves the no effect model is impossible.
column4: A very small chance value suggests the data are unusual.
column5: A very small chance value can support a treatment effect.
column6: A very small chance value can challenge chance as the explanation.

column2: Why does random assignment matter in a significance test for a treatment?
column3: It makes the sample representative of all people.
column4: It supports comparing groups as if chance assigned them.
column5: It guarantees the difference in means is zero.
column6: It ensures the population standard deviation is known.

column2: If subjects are volunteers but treatments are randomized what is limited?
column3: The ability to compare groups fairly is limited.
column4: The ability to estimate an unusual result is limited.
column5: The ability to infer a cause for the subjects is limited.
column6: The ability to generalize to all students is limited.

column2: If a study has no random assignment what should you avoid concluding?
column3: Avoid concluding the data show any difference.
column4: Avoid concluding the graph has any spread.
column5: Avoid concluding the treatment caused the difference.
column6: Avoid concluding the sample came from volunteers.

column2: In a test for a difference in means what counts as evidence for the claim?
column3: A sample statistic close to the no effect value.
column4: A sample statistic in the direction of the claim.
column5: A sample statistic with no variation at all.
column6: A sample statistic from a perfectly normal graph.

column2: Why does the probability include results more extreme than observed?
column3: Those results would support the claim at least as much.
column4: Those results keep the graph centered at zero.
column5: Those results make the sample more representative.
column6: Those results remove the need for random assignment.

column2: If results like the observed one are common in the simulation what should you conclude?
column3: Conclude the treatment works for every subject.
column4: Conclude the sample statistic must be biased.
column5: Conclude the no effect model has been disproved.
column6: Conclude chance remains a reasonable explanation.

column2: Which observed result would be most surprising under a no effect model?
column3: A result near the center of the simulated graph.
column4: A result close to zero on the simulated graph.
column5: A result deep in the tail of the simulated graph.
column6: A result that matches many simulated values.

column2: How is a significance test different from a simple sample comparison?
column3: It asks whether chance alone could explain the difference.
column4: It asks whether the sample mean equals the parameter.
column5: It asks whether the graph is exactly bell shaped.
column6: It asks whether the sample size is large enough.

column2: Which statement shows the mistake of ignoring chance variation?
column3: The sample difference is one piece of evidence to weigh.
column4: The sample difference is not zero so the treatment worked.
column5: The sample difference should be compared with a chance model.
column6: The sample difference may still happen even under no effect.

column2: If the no effect model is true where should simulated differences usually be centered?
column3: They should be centered near the sample difference.
column4: They should be centered near the claim value.
column5: They should be centered near the largest value.
column6: They should be centered near zero difference.

column2: Why are many simulation trials used instead of just a few?
column3: They make each trial less random than before.
column4: They make the observed difference become larger.
column5: They make the tail probability estimate more stable.
column6: They make the study conclusions automatically causal.

column2: In this lesson what does convincing evidence against no effect mean?
column3: The observed result matches the center of the model.
column4: The observed result is rare under the chance-only model.
column5: The observed result removes all uncertainty from the study.
column6: The observed result guarantees a large practical effect.

column2: Which statement best describes the probability estimated by the simulation?
column3: It is the chance of results this extreme under no effect.
column4: It is the chance the treatment helped every subject.
column5: It is the chance the sample mean equals the parameter.
column6: It is the chance the study design had no flaws.

column2: If the estimated chance is not small what is the safest conclusion?
column3: The treatment definitely has no effect at all.
column4: The random assignment must have failed badly.
column5: The no effect model has been proved correct forever.
column6: The data do not rule out chance as the explanation.

column2: What should come first when using significance test logic?
column3: State that the claim must already be true.
column4: State that the sample result is statistically significant.
column5: State what outcomes are expected if no effect is true.
column6: State which future sample will be collected next.
